summary: An early working paper on how hosts on the ARPANET might account for and administer network use, such as who is charged for what. It does not take a position; it identifies the issues for further discussion, considering current practices and new technical possibilities.

eli5.summary: If many people share a pool, someone must decide who pays. This note lists the questions without picking an answer yet.

subtitle: Identifying the questions for billing and administration in a shared network

tldr.problem: As multiple institutions share the ARPANET, someone must decide how to account for resource usage and charge for it, but no policy yet exists.
tldr.mechanism: This early working paper identifies the key questions to answer: who operates the network, what are the charging policies, and what technical support do they require.
tldr.outcome: The RFC lists issues for community discussion without recommending answers, establishing the framework for future billing standards.

today: RFC 136 was a working paper that opened discussion. No single standardized billing scheme for the ARPANET was ever mandated; each site developed its own accounting practices.

sections.title: The Accounting Problem
sections.content: The ARPANET is growing and now includes multiple hosts run by different organizations. Some way must be found to track how much each host uses the network and who should pay for it. The RFC is an early working paper; it identifies the questions without proposing answers.
sections.eli5: A shared network needs rules for who pays. This note asks the questions without answering them yet.

sections.title: The Assumptions
sections.content: The author sets out three groups of assumptions for how the network might be operated. For the subnet (the IMPs and links), some entity should operate it as a cost center and charge the host sites. Each host would arrange billing with the institutions it serves. Both ARPA-sponsored and non-ARPA sites would eventually be allowed to connect. The network is not a common carrier but a resource-sharing network for its participants.
sections.eli5: The note assumes someone will run the network and charge fees, hosts will figure out their own rates, and many kinds of organizations will join.

sections.title: Topics for Decision
sections.content: The RFC then lists topics the network community should discuss: How do hosts currently do accounting? What access and security rules should apply? Should host accounting and network accounting be independent? What charging policies make sense? Should certain activities be free? Finally, should accounting flow through the network itself, in real time? These questions have no obvious answers, and the RFC encourages the community to propose more topics.
sections.eli5: The note asks: how do we charge for what? How much should it be? Can we measure it automatically? Should some things be free?
